title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 3: Global Support for Judicial Reforms
keywords: consul ad honorem of the Republic of Honduras
Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary
Strengthening the Independence and Defining the Accountability of the Judiciary
Access to Justice for the Poor through Information, Education and Communication (IEC)
International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- a luncheon address to the Consular Corps of the Philippines in which CJP catalogues, donor by donor, the extraordinary breadth of international support the Philippine judiciary's Action Program for Judicial Reform has attracted.

The APJR itself: approved by the Supreme Court on December 8, 2000 to realize the 'Davide Watch' vision, it addresses nine concerns of the Philippine judiciary and reduces to three targets CJP labels 'CID' -- corruption, incompetence and delay.

A systematic roll-call of eleven foreign partners -- UNDP, World Bank, ADB, USAID, The Asia Foundation, CIDA, AusAID, the European Union, Japan, Britain and the Netherlands -- with the concrete projects each has financed.

The forthcoming International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms of November 28-30, 2005, and the Asia-Pacific Judicial Reform Network it is expected to launch, for which CJP as conference chairman solicits the consuls' help in inviting their home judiciaries.
sub_topics: CJP opens with the personal note that he was himself once a member of the consular corps as consul ad honorem of the Republic of Honduras, making the luncheon 'a long overdue reunion.'
He traces the reform program to the 'Davide Watch' enunciated by Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. on assuming office on November 30, 1998.
The APJR, approved December 8, 2000, is described as comprehensive and wide-ranging, addressing nine enumerated problems from case congestion to limited access to justice by the poor.

The nine problems are compressed into the 'CID' memory guide -- corruption, incompetence and delay -- and pursued through more than 100 specific projects coordinated by the Court's Program Management Office.
The program's premise: stability and predictability in the dispensation of justice are requirements of good governance, which is in turn a prerequisite of economic development.
UNDP funded the 'Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary' from which the APJR descends, plus access-to-justice studies, jail decongestion with the IBP, Shari'a court strengthening and gender-bias work.

The World Bank's Judicial Reform Support Program funded the e-library, computer-aided transcription, an infrastructure master plan, case decongestion, the 'Justice on Wheels' mobile court, model electronic courts and the GSIS building's conversion into a Manila Hall of Justice.

World Bank-sponsored study visits by SC justices seeded case computerization, the e-library, mobile courts and e-docket payments here -- and gave birth to the idea of the International Conference and Showcase itself.
The ADB granted over US$1 million for the study 'Strengthening the Independence and Defining the Accountability of the Judiciary,' plus environmental-law forums and a Japan training course.

USAID assisted about 30 reform activities, including the Pasay City Case Flow Management Pilot Project, a uniform writing-style manual, Justice-to-Justice and Judge-to-Judge dialogues and judicial ethics symposia.
The Asia Foundation supported 'Chamber to Chamber' Dialogues with the business community, a law-student apprenticeship program and the PERLAS rule-of-law education project.

CIDA gave a Canadian $7 million grant for the CAMIS case-tracking project, training at the Commonwealth Judicial Education Institute in Halifax, computers for Philja and the JURIS project's mediation, education and advocacy components.
AusAID financed the Benchbook for Trial Court Judges, a training needs assessment and the 'Justice Link' citizens' feedback mechanism.
The European Union gave 2.73 million euros for 'Access to Justice for the Poor through Information, Education and Communication' (2005-2008) and for courts serving internally displaced persons.

Japan is in final negotiations for a P600 million grant to build the Philja Training Center in Tagaytay; the British Council funded the National Forum on the Five Pillars of Justice; the Netherlands funded baseline studies.

The International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms is described as a three-day gathering of plenary and parallel sessions plus an exhibit, with donor funding covering fee-free participation for chief justices of about 80 countries and roughly 150 invited participants.
Participants are expected to establish an Asia-Pacific Judicial Reform Network as the institutional vehicle for continuing the conference's initiatives.
CJP closes by thanking the international community and asking the consuls to relay the invitation to their own judiciaries.

stances.claim: The observance of the rule of law is not a luxury but an economic necessity: stability and predictability in the dispensation of justice are indispensable requirements of good governance, which is in turn a prerequisite of economic development.
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-of-law-as-economic-infrastructure: binding speedy justice, democracy and the economy into 'one tapestry of governance' to justify reform spending to a diplomatic and business-facing audience

stances.claim: The Philippine judiciary's reform program has attracted a degree of global assistance unmatched anywhere, and that support obliges the Court to see the reforms through to the speedy delivery of quality justice.
stances.rhetorical_move: donor-by-donor enumeration: eleven partners and their named projects are recited in sequence as evidence, then converted into a vow of gratitude and follow-through

stances.claim: The APJR's many disparate projects are best understood as an attack on three problems -- corruption, incompetence and delay -- which CJP packages as the 'CID' targets of judicial reform.
stances.rhetorical_move: mnemonic compression: a nine-item problem list is reduced to a three-letter memory guide so a lay audience can carry the reform agenda away

stances.claim: The forthcoming International Conference and Showcase is worth the consuls' effort because judiciaries need to share reform knowledge with each other, and the Philippine program is acclaimed enough to be worth showing.
stances.rhetorical_move: invitation-as-peroration: the catalogue of donor support becomes the credential that licenses a direct request that the consuls invite their home judiciaries

notable_anecdotes: CJP discloses that long before joining the Supreme Court he was consul ad honorem of the Republic of Honduras, so that addressing the Consular Corps was for him 'really a long overdue reunion.'

He names the two consuls behind the invitation -- former Tourism Secretary and Ivory Coast Honorary Consul Vince Carlos, who first broached the idea, and Her Majesty's Consul John Fielder, who wrote asking him to speak on judicial reform.

He recounts that the idea of the International Conference and Showcase was born during World Bank-sponsored visits by SC justices to other jurisdictions, out of the perceived need of various countries to share reform projects among themselves.
He reports that the Court's first mobile court under the 'Justice on Wheels' program had already made an impact on decongesting jails and speedily resolving family problems in Metro Manila.

He notes that the World Bank had 'generously acceded' to finance the rehabilitation of the old GSIS building on Arroceros Street in Manila for conversion into a modern Hall of Justice for Manila trial courts.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces a luncheon address Justice Panganiban gave to the Consular Corps of the Philippines, whose dean, Her Majesty's Consul John Fielder, had asked him to speak on the Supreme Court's judicial reforms and the coming International Conference and Showcase; he opened by noting that he had himself once been consul ad honorem of the Republic of Honduras, making the occasion a reunion. He traced the reform effort to the 'Davide Watch' that Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. enunciated on assuming office on November 30, 1998, and to the Action Program for Judicial Reform the Court approved on December 8, 2000, which addresses nine problems ranging from case congestion and budget deficiency to perceived corruption and limited access to justice by the poor, and which he compressed into a three-letter memory guide, the 'CID' targets -- corruption, incompetence and delay -- pursued through more than 100 projects coordinated by the Court's Program Management Office. He grounded the program in the proposition that stability and predictability in the dispensation of justice are indispensable requirements of good governance and hence a prerequisite of economic development, since speedy justice, democracy and the economy are intertwined into one tapestry of governance. The bulk of the speech was a donor-by-donor inventory: UNDP's Blueprint of Action and access-to-justice studies; the World Bank's Judicial Reform Support Program, e-library, computer-aided transcription, model electronic courts, 'Justice on Wheels' and the GSIS-building Hall of Justice; the ADB's million-dollar independence-and-accountability study; some thirty USAID activities; The Asia Foundation's Chamber-to-Chamber dialogues and PERLAS; CIDA's CAMIS grant and JURIS project; AusAID's Benchbook and Justice Link; the EU's 2.73-million-euro access-to-justice grant; and Japanese, British and Dutch support. He closed by saying he knew of no other country enjoying a similar degree of global assistance, vowing to pursue the reforms to completion, and inviting the consuls to bring their own judiciaries to the November 28-30, 2005 conference, which was expected to establish an Asia-Pacific Judicial Reform Network.
